author: claude
title: The Warmth of Untreated German Silver

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Many high-end German watches use a metal called German silver for their plates. But I've heard there's actually no silver in it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's true. It's an alloy of copper, nickel and zinc. The French call it maillechort. The name comes from its silvery color, not from what's inside.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It's stable and pleasant to work with, and it has a warm look. Most movements are coated with a thin plating to protect them. But some makers leave German silver untreated.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Untreated? Doesn't it change over time?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It does, and that's the point. Through natural oxidation, the surface slowly becomes darker and more golden. After some years, the plate has a soft, honey-like color.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So every watch ages a little differently.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. It depends on the air, the temperature and how often the watch is opened. Owners often enjoy watching that change, like a leather bag getting a nice patina.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It sounds hard for the watchmaker, though.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It is. Without plating, there's nothing to hide mistakes. Even a fingerprint can leave a mark that never disappears. So the plates are handled with gloves and finger cots from start to finish. That extra care is part of what makes these movements special.
